parent.text: A few thoughts on the Coldcard security incident (in no particular order): 1. This is devastating for a lot of people. They lost their hard-earned economic value in a way most didn’t realize was possible. Not everyone is a technical genius, but almost all are merely looking to build a better life for themselves and their family. I feel for these people and their new reality. 2. I have personally lost bitcoin in the past and it is never fun. The only lesson I can impart from my personal experience on those going through this is that you are unlikely to change the past. Don’t spend immense time thinking about what could have been, but rather focus on a plan moving forward. You can only control your actions and response, so focus on how to come back stronger. 3. People will inevitably attack the various investors in Coldcard, or the podcasters promoting the product, but that anger is misplaced and unproductive. I saw this phenomenon first-hand with the BlockFi situation. Even though I wasn’t involved in the company’s operations, people wanted someone to blame and they came for those who were the most accessible. To those who are angry, don’t waste your time attacking those who are not responsible. To those who will be unjustly attacked, this too shall pass. 4. This incident highlights the difficulty with self-custody. I fundamentally believe in an individual’s right to have true sovereignty over their assets. It is one of the core value propositions of bitcoin. But we must also recognize that self-custody is a technically complex topic that some, but not all, are prepared to take on. Better education and better technology can help bridge this gap in the future. 5. The mainstream media hasn’t picked up this story yet, but I am sure they will at some point. They can’t resist the “bitcoin was hacked!” storyline. Obviously bitcoin was not hacked and there is no known security vulnerability with the protocol. This was a third-party issue, but that won’t stop the misinformation, so it is important to combat the misinformation with facts. 6. Sentiment in the bitcoin industry is very bad right now. This is normal in a bear market, so it is not surprising. But a security incident like this is equivalent to throwing a match on gasoline. There will be more anger, in-fighting, and unproductive nonsense. If this is your first time experiencing it, welcome to the arena. If you have seen it before, you know the negative sentiment will eventually evaporate and the sun will shine again over the next 12-18 months. 7. There are very real ramifications to the acceleration in AI technology. I am not sure if AI played a part in this hack, but it wouldn’t surprise me if that was the case. Every developer should take this new capability seriously and consider how they can enhance their security practices accordingly. 8. The bitcoin community is just as resilient as the network itself. We have been through insane, painful moments throughout the years. This is another one. The only way forward is to go through the fire. In conclusion, this situation sucks for everyone affected. I genuinely feel for you and intimately understand the pain from my own past experiences. Keep your head up and continue walking forward. Love you all ❤️

parent.text: One of the reasons I started posting here was that I despised and was sickened by some of the trash that was being spouted by so-called option gurus trying to get paid-subs. There are times when the Funkyness of options during extreme events occurs, where the logic of anything you may have read/learnt and certainly been sold falls apart. Options ARE complex, I hold the unpopular opinion that most of Option trading should be Experts only. 'Searching for strikes is not intuitive, the wall of numbers is overwhelming - you came here to express a view and suddenly you’re learning greeks… WTAF?' - @fiddybps1 0DTE options have become such a success in tradfi markets because they eliminate much of the complexity of greeks and satisfy dopamine needs. There are instances, however, of non-experts producing incredible returns in mid-long term time frames. The convex payoff of options, above other products, and the fixed downside loss enables buying options at cheap implied vol levels to express a directional view THE smart strategy. I use 'non-experts' respectfully; all are super smart, but some, if not most, will admit to little options technical knowledge or experience. @koolkrypto223 - 'I don't even have a TradFi/options trading background, I effectively taught myself earlier this year.' - [Btw impressive and employs AI to route out potential trade outcomes pre-expiry; previously not a simple thing to do and rarely do any trades reach expiry, so under-rated]. Other non-tradfi but the big-name crypto specialists such as @ThinkingUSD, @lightcrypto, @cobie, @Rewkang @thiccyth0t, @crypto_condom have employed options very successfully over the years. Ultimately, what separates them from others is their underlying THESIS AND TIMING, not their knowledge of the greeks. But this 'timing' often resulted in them buying options when Implied vol was cheap, ie pre-move, low realized vol, defined by their thesis. When IV was a little higher such as HYPE, Call spreads mitigated the Vega, but the thinking behind this was - I'm guessing - that higher call leg looks out of scope, let's lessen the cost - ie common sense rather than checking out the expected Vega reaction of the Skew as the Call spread rallied. So Options have their place. Have a thesis. Time it. Buy cheap vol. Convex results. Otherwise you're edging into just gambling or FOMO. Strike selection and Expiry overcomplicate - it's generally all maths, and they are highly related; but give yourself sufficient time. CLOB are too difficult to navigate for non-experts. RFQ works nicely. Exiting ITM options is a failure place for onchain. If buying in size, you will be encouraged to sell an upper strike - solves margin for MM and allows the MM to take advantage of you on two legs! Quote multiple places. And don't just look at payoff returns: it looks nice to have a call spread with a 30x payoff to outlay, but take out the higher strike you have sold and effectively you have an infinite upside. The key is not just payoff rr but probability. I apologise to anyone I have named here that disagrees with me calling them super smart or giving them any respect that they know what an option is even at the most retarded level.

parent.text: At my new job, a lot of coworkers used to work at an Elon co. And tbh, I keep hearing pieces of his management style that sound effective & I’m not sure why other companies don’t apply them. Main idea: the leader of quite a large group can & should very much have daily/weekly meetings with a bunch of ICs where they align & push. Eg: Elon being very involved with Grok training. In practice, even in 10-20 eng startups, or 40 eng orgs at large companies, this really isn’t the case! There’s an unnecessary level of delegation that seems to dilute speed & alignment. The leader just doesn’t know what’s going on, how fast or slow things need to take, whether the right thing is being built. Like: when I think about the company I used to work at, Series A, 20 people, I think we could have been a lot more effective with frequent opinionation, product vision, alignment, pressure from the CEO. This company is quite small you really shouldn’t be delegating! This might sound like micromanaging, but really, more small teams should think of themselves as instruments wielded & oriented by a clear eyed one. I think at most teams I’ve been on, the executive vision was good enough that executing on it faster would just work! Vs slowly meandering in many directions. I think you could do this without too much harshness towards your team either, you’d mostly just need the harshness towards yourself. I think folks get too lazy to be on top of all the details they’d need to know to orchestrate their team, and justify this to themselves by claiming to want to provide autonomy.

parent.text: Not discrediting what Hyperliquid has achieved - clearly it's both a major source of liquidity and price discovery, as shown with several ~$1B positions having been opened (congrats!) - but this type of surface level comparison of book depth as a measure of liquidity is pretty misleading. $1 in HL OB ≠ $1 in Binance OB. Hyperliquid implements a "speedbump" (cancel orders have priority against taker orders) so essentially any maker can place orders of size, in which they have no intention of filling. In contrast to Binance, there is no way really to duck from an incoming order because i) you don't see it and ii) the cancellation vs new order placement latency is very similar. These two factors make it much easier to get picked off providing liquidity. As an example, if we take a recent short-term movement in ETH perps from today at 9:41PM UTC, likely led by Binance, you can see quite clearly the difference in the actual available liquidity across exchanges for this period. Hyperliquid, having only ~$2.5M volume, is working by design to combat "toxic takers". What may have been ~$20m at ±0.7% book depth liquidity starting from $2,914 (before the move upwards) has largely been cancelled, leading to very few matches and thus low volume. Looking at only the :22 bubbles, other CEXs show a substantially larger amount of liquidity being taken, despite their order books not appearing “as liquid.” Just as you wouldn't say "it only takes $2.5M to move ETH 0.70% on HL" (true here under these conditions, but generally not), you also wouldn't compare these orderbooks in the first place as they have completely different properties!
